```{r, include = FALSE}
has_spatstat <- requireNamespace("spatstat.explore", quietly = TRUE) &&

```

A map can suggest that a gene clusters, or that a clone stays in one place.
A spatial statistic tells you whether the pattern is stronger than chance.
SIRUP has five tests. Each one answers a different question:

| Question | Function | Statistic |
|---|---|---|
| Does one variable cluster in space? | `spatialMoran()` | Global Moran's I |
| Where are the clusters? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | Local Moran's I |
| Do two variables have the same spatial pattern? | `spatialLee()` | Lee's L |
| Are spots of type A near spots of type B? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | Ripley's cross K |
| Do the spots of one clone sit next to each other? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Join count |

`spatialCloneSpread()` also measures how far each clone spreads across a
section.

The tests use the spdep and spatstat packages. Each one accepts a SIRUP object
and reads the spot coordinates and image settings from it. The examples use MG
thymus section 2.

## Set up

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r setup}
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")
read_receptors <- function(file, locus) {
  airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>%
    extractSpatialIds(
      id = "sequence_id",
      spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
      regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
      suffix = "-1"
    ) %>%
    filterAirr(
      locus_val = locus,
      min_v_length = 250,
      min_j_length = 30,
      min_junction_length = 10,
      productive_only = TRUE,
      min_consensus_count = NULL,
      spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
    ) %>%
    filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
}

thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))

cell_types <- data.table::fread(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"),
  data.table = FALSE
) %>%
  filter(sample == "mg_thymus_slice2")
rownames(cell_types) <- cell_types$barcode
thymus <- Seurat::AddMetaData(thymus, select(cell_types, -sample, -barcode))

bcr_sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = read_receptors("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "IGH"),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
bcr_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  bcr_sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)

tcr_sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = read_receptors("mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz", "TRB"),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
tcr_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tcr_sirup,
  scoper::identicalClones,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

`read_receptors()` reads a consensus table, takes the spot barcode from
`sequence_id`, and keeps the high-quality sequences of one locus with
unambiguous junctions. BCR clones come from `scoper::hierarchicalClones()`.
TCRs do not mutate, so TCR clones come from `scoper::identicalClones()`.

## Neighbors

Most of these statistics compare each spot with its neighbors. You choose the
neighbors in one of two ways:

* `k`: the `k` nearest spots. Use `k = 6` for standard Visium, where each spot
  has six neighbors on a hexagonal grid. Use `k = 8` for Visium HD, where each
  bin has eight neighbors on a square grid. Larger values of `k` measure
  patterns over larger distances.
* `radius`: all spots within a distance. SIRUP measures distances in image
  pixels at the stored `image_scale`, so the same radius in micrometers needs
  a different number at `"lowres"` and at `"hires"`.

`k` does not depend on the image scale, so it is the safer default.

## Global Moran's I

Moran's I measures spatial autocorrelation: whether neighboring spots have
similar values.

$$
I = \frac{N}{W} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
$$

Here $x_i$ is the value at spot $i$, $w_{ij}$ is 1 if spot $j$ is a neighbor
of spot $i$ and 0 if not, $N$ is the number of spots, and $W$ is the sum of
all $w_{ij}$. $I$ near 0 means no spatial pattern. Positive $I$ means that
similar values cluster. Negative $I$ means that they alternate, as on a
chessboard.

`variable_type` tells SIRUP what `variable` is:

* `"feature"`: a gene, from the assay and layer you give.
* `"metadata"`: a numeric spot metadata column. For a text column, give
  `value` to test the spots that have that value.
* `"receptor"`: 1 for spots with any receptor and 0 for other spots.
  `variable` is only a label here.
* `"clone"`: 1 for spots with the clone that `variable` names.

```{r moran}
aicda <- spatialMoran(
  bcr_sirup,
  variable = "AICDA",
  variable_type = "feature",
  assay = "Spatial",
  layer = "data",
  k = 6
)
aicda$test
```

The result is a list. `test` is the `spdep::moran.test()` result: the
statistic, its expected value under no spatial pattern, the variance, and the
p value. For *AICDA*, $I$ is small (0.06) but the p value is below $10^{-9}$.
Visium detects *AICDA* in few spots, and most spots have a count of zero, so
the clustering is real but weak. Read $I$ for the size of the pattern and
the p value for the evidence.

The same function tests cell-type proportions and receptor presence:

```{r moran-more}
moran_table <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "AICDA expression", I = aicda$test$estimate[[1]], p = aicda$test$p.value),
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(bcr_sirup, variable = "GC B", variable_type = "metadata", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "GC B cell proportion", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  },
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(bcr_sirup, variable = "BCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "BCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  },
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(tcr_sirup, variable = "TCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "TCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  }
)
moran_table
```

The GC B cell proportion clusters more strongly ($I$ = 0.62): the
cell2location estimate is smooth and has no zeros from sampling. A p value of
0 means a value below the smallest number that R can store.

Moran's I works for binary variables, such as receptor presence, but the
join-count test below suits them better.

## Local Moran's I

Global Moran's I gives one number for the whole section. Local Moran's I
(also called LISA) gives one value for each spot. A spot with a high positive
value has a high (or low) value itself and neighbors with similar values. Its
z-score shows how far it is from the value expected by chance.

```{r local-moran}
gc_b_local <- spatialLocalMoran(
  bcr_sirup,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
head(gc_b_local[, c("cell", "value", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
```

`plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue. Red spots are in
clusters of similar values. Blue spots differ from their neighbors:

```{r local-moran-plot}
plotSpatialLocalMoran(
  bcr_sirup,
  gc_b_local,
  point_size = 1,
  title = "GC B cell proportion, local Moran's I (z-score)"
) +
  labs(color = "z")
```

The clusters of high GC B cell proportion sit where we drew the eGC polygons.
Each spot has its own p value, so correct for multiple testing (for example
with `p.adjust(method = "BH")`) before you call a spot significant.

## Lee's L: two variables

Lee's L combines Pearson correlation with spatial smoothing. It is high when
two variables are high in the same neighborhoods, even if they do not peak in
the same spots.

In MG, patients make antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR).
*CHRNA1* codes for the AChR α subunit. Thymic myoid cells express it. Lee's L
tests whether *CHRNA1* and the GC marker *AICDA* share a spatial pattern in
this section. *MS4A1* (CD20) gives a positive control, because GC B cells
express both *MS4A1* and *AICDA*:

```{r lee}
lee_control <- spatialLee(
  bcr_sirup,
  x = "AICDA", y = "MS4A1",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6
)
lee_chrna1 <- spatialLee(
  bcr_sirup,
  x = "AICDA", y = "CHRNA1",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6
)

tibble(
  pair = c("AICDA and MS4A1", "AICDA and CHRNA1"),
  L = c(lee_control$L, lee_chrna1$L),
  p = c(lee_control$test$p.value, lee_chrna1$test$p.value)
)
```

The control pair shares a pattern. *AICDA* and *CHRNA1* do not: in this
section, $L$ is near zero and the test is not significant.

The analytical test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one
entry for each pair of spots. That is fine for Visium. For Visium HD, use
`method = "mc"`, which uses permutations and sparse weights.

## Ripley's cross K: are A spots near B spots?

Ripley's cross K counts, for each distance $r$, how many type B points are
within $r$ of an average type A point:

$$
K_{AB}(r) = \frac{|W|}{N_A N_B} \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} \mathbf{1}(d_{ij} \le r)
$$

$|W|$ is the area of the tissue window and $d_{ij}$ is the distance between
points $i$ and $j$. SIRUP compares the observed curve with curves from random
relabeling of the points. If the observed curve is above the envelope of the
random curves, A and B are closer than chance.

T follicular helper (Tfh) cells give B cells the signals that keep a
germinal center going. Here we ask whether spots with GC B cells sit near
spots with Tfh cells. First, label each spot from its cell2location
proportions. `updateSpatial()` runs a function on the Seurat object and stores
the result:

```{r ripley-marks}
bcr_sirup <- updateSpatial(bcr_sirup, function(spatial) {
  gc_b <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10
  tfh <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10
  spatial$gc_tfh_mark <- case_when(
    gc_b & !tfh ~ "GC B",
    tfh & !gc_b ~ "Tfh",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
  spatial
})

table(getSpatial(bcr_sirup)$gc_tfh_mark, useNA = "ifany")
```

Spots with neither cell type, or with both, get `NA`, and the test leaves them
out. Then run the test. `nsim` sets the number of random relabelings. Use 99 or
more for a final analysis:

```{r ripley, eval = has_spatstat, results = "hide"}
gc_tfh_k <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  bcr_sirup,
  mark_col = "gc_tfh_mark",
  i = "GC B",
  j = "Tfh",
  nsim = 39,
  max_r = 40
)

plotRipleyCrossK(gc_tfh_k, title = "Cross K: GC B spots to Tfh spots")
```

The distance $r$ is in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. To convert it
to micrometers, use the Visium spot size. A spot is 55 µm wide, and the image
object stores its diameter in full-resolution pixels:

```{r microns, eval = has_spatstat}
scale_factors <- getSpatial(bcr_sirup)@images[[1]]@scale.factors
um_per_pixel <- 55 / (scale_factors$spot * scale_factors$lowres)
um_per_pixel
max(gc_tfh_k$plot_data$r) * um_per_pixel
```

So `max_r = 40` lowres pixels is about 470 µm.

In this section the observed curve is below the envelope at every distance.
Random relabeling keeps the marked spots where they are and shuffles the
labels. A curve below the envelope therefore means that GC B spots sit next
to other GC B spots, and Tfh spots next to other Tfh spots, more often than
next to each other. The two cell types form separate groups at the 10%
threshold. The rule that drops spots with both cell types adds to the
separation. Change the thresholds or the marks to ask a different question.

## Join counts: does a clone stay together?

The join-count test is the natural test for a clone. Take every spot with a
BCR. Mark the spots that have the clone. Count the neighbor pairs in which
both spots have the clone (the "joins"). If the clone stays in one place,
there are more joins than random labeling gives.

`spatialCloneJoinCount()` runs `spdep::joincount.test()` for each clone in at
least `min_spatial_ids` spots. When the object has stored polygons, the
function runs one test per polygon by default. Set
`use_stored_polygons = FALSE` for one test over the whole section:

```{r join-count}
big_clones <- getReceptors(bcr_sirup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(barcode_10x)) %>%
  distinct(clone_id, barcode_10x) %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(clone_id)

join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  bcr_sirup,
  clone_val = big_clones,
  use_stored_polygons = FALSE,
  k = 6,
  return_data = TRUE
)

join_count$summary
```

The summary has one row per clone. `statistic` is the standardized join count
(a z-score) and `p_value` is the one-sided p value.
`plotSpatialCloneJoinCount()` shows the clone and the joins:

```{r join-count-plot}
plotSpatialCloneJoinCount(
  join_count = join_count,
  object = bcr_sirup,
  clone_val = join_count$summary$clone_id[[1]],
  show_neighbors = TRUE
)
```

The plot needs `return_data = TRUE` in the test.

## Clone spread

`spatialCloneSpread()` describes how far each clone reaches across the section,
from the pairwise distances between its sequences:

```{r spread}
spread <- spatialCloneSpread(bcr_sirup, min_spatial_ids = 3)
spread %>%
  arrange(desc(n_spatial_ids)) %>%
  head()
```

The distances are in image pixels. By default, sequences in the same spot
count as separate points at distance 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to
count each spot once.

## Keep the results

Store results that you want to keep in the object, so they travel with the
data:

```{r store}
bcr_sirup <- bcr_sirup %>%
  setAnalysis("moran_aicda", aicda) %>%
  setAnalysis("local_moran_gc_b", gc_b_local) %>%
  setAnalysis("lee_aicda_chrna1", lee_chrna1) %>%
  setAnalysis("clone_join_count", join_count) %>%
  setAnalysis("clone_spread", spread)
listAnalyses(bcr_sirup)
```
